case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an issuer’s mere failure to make a disclosure required by SEC Regulation S‑K Item 303 (MD&A) can, by itself and without rendering any affirmative statement misleading, support a private securities-fraud claim under Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b‑5.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and SEC Rule 10b-5 (with Item 303 of Regulation S‑K as the alleged source of a disclosure duty; related implications for Securities Act §§11 and 12(a)(2) claims premised on Item 303 omissions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Rule 10b‑5(b) targets misleading statements (and half-truths), not pure omissions absent a separate duty to speak that makes silence misleading; Item 303 is an SEC disclosure regime enforced primarily by the SEC and does not automatically create a privately enforceable duty whose violation is securities fraud. They contend the Second Circuit wrongly allowed plaintiffs to plead a 10b‑5 claim based solely on an Item 303 omission, expanding private liability beyond the text and structure of §10(b)/Rule 10b‑5 and conflicting with other circuits, while creating significant uncertainty and over-deterrence around MD&A disclosures.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Moab) argue that Item 303 imposes a mandatory disclosure duty regarding known trends/uncertainties, and that when such required information is omitted from public filings, the omission can be actionable under Rule 10b‑5 so long as plaintiffs independently plead the rest of the elements of a 10b‑5 claim (materiality, scienter, reliance, loss causation, etc.). They emphasize that Rule 10b‑5 liability can rest on omissions where there is a duty to disclose, and Item 303 supplies that duty; they also frame the case as properly interlocutory because the Second Circuit’s rule aligns with the traditional “duty to disclose” concept and can be applied without converting every Item 303 issue into automatic liability.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Item 303 supplies the “duty to disclose” referenced in Basic, but that reading would effectively convert every SEC line-item duty into privately enforceable 10b-5 omission liability—an expansion Santa Fe cautions against and that sits uneasily with Rule 10b-5(b)’s own limitation to omissions needed to keep “statements made” from being misleading. Justice Kavanaugh’s structural contrast to Securities Act §11’s express “required to be stated” language is especially persuasive evidence that Congress knew how to impose freestanding omission liability and did not do so in §10(b), which counsels a narrow construction of the implied private action. Justice Sotomayor’s point about Chiarella/Dirks further reinforces that our omission cases tie liability to duties that make silence deceptive in context (fiduciary/half-truth), not mere regulatory noncompliance. The narrow, institutionally legitimate rule is therefore that Item 303 can inform whether an affirmative statement is misleading, but an Item 303 omission alone is not actionable under §10(b)/Rule 10b-5(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest possible respondent argument is that Basic’s “silence, absent a duty to disclose, is not misleading” could treat Item 303 as supplying the relevant duty; but §10(b)’s text limits liability to “manipulative or deceptive” devices, and Rule 10b-5(b) limits omissions to those “necessary in order to make the statements made … not misleading,” not to any fact an SEC rule might require. Justice Kavanaugh’s contrast to Securities Act §11—which expressly covers omission of facts “required to be stated”—reinforces that Congress did not adopt that broader omission theory in §10(b), so courts should not expand the implied private action beyond deception. Santa Fe confirms we may not convert §10(b) into a general code for regulatory noncompliance, and Chiarella/Dirks ground omission liability in duties that make silence deceptive in context (fiduciary/half-truth), not in every disclosure-item mandate. Accordingly, a bare Item 303 omission untethered to a misleading affirmative statement is not actionable under §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 in a private suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Item 303 supplies the “duty to disclose” referenced in Basic, making silence deceptive; but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Rule 10b-5(b) textually limits omission liability to what is necessary to make “statements made” not misleading, not to every regulatory line-item a filer fails to include. Justice Kavanaugh’s comparison to Securities Act §11’s express “required to be stated” omission language is powerful structural evidence that Congress chose not to create freestanding omission liability under §10(b), and Santa Fe cautions us against turning the implied 10b-5 action into a general disclosure-enforcement regime. Chiarella/Dirks further confirm that actionable silence in §10(b) is tied to duties that make nondisclosure deceptive in context (fiduciary/half-truth), so Item 303 can inform whether an affirmative statement is misleading but cannot itself be a standalone private-fraud trigger. The practical consequences also cut strongly against respondent: automatic private 10b-5 exposure for Item 303 would invite hindsight-heavy MD&A litigation better left to SEC calibration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that Item 303 supplies the “duty to disclose” contemplated by Basic, making silence deceptive; but Rule 10b-5(b) still textually limits omission liability to what is necessary to keep the issuer’s actual statements from being misleading, so regulatory noncompliance alone can’t do the work of deception. Justice Kagan’s workability concern resonates with my pragmatic approach: turning MD&A’s management-oriented, judgment-laden discussion into automatic private-fraud exposure would predictably over-deter and distort disclosures, with the heaviest costs falling on ordinary and vulnerable investors who bear market-wide compliance and litigation burdens. Justice Kavanaugh’s contrast to Securities Act §11’s express “required to be stated” language underscores the institutional point that Congress chose a different liability trigger there than in §10(b), so we should not expand the implied private action beyond half-truths and similar deceptive contexts recognized in Chiarella/Dirks. Investors still get meaningful protection because Item 303 omissions remain actionable when they render affirmative statements misleading, while pure Item 303 lapses remain chiefly for SEC enforcement.

Nothing in Chiarella/Dirks, as Justice Sotomayor notes, suggests that a line-item regulatory obligation alone creates the kind of transaction-linked duty whose breach is “deceptive” in the §10(b) sense.

Chiarella and Dirks further confirm that actionable silence under §10(b) is tied to fiduciary-like duties or half-truths, not mere regulatory noncompliance, so Item 303 can inform whether an affirmative statement was misleading but cannot, standing alone, create private 10b-5(b) liability. No colleague’s cited precedent undermines that reading; if anything, Chief Justice Roberts’s point that importing all regulatory duties would “federalize” disclosure enforcement reinforces the institutional limits built into the text.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 10(b) reaches only “manipulative or deceptive” conduct, and Rule 10b-5(b) likewise targets omissions only when they make “statements made” misleading; a freestanding failure to comply with Item 303’s MD&A requirements is therefore regulatory noncompliance, not necessarily deception. Santa Fe Industries, Inc. v. Green cautions against “judicially extend[ing]” §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 to cover breaches of duty untethered to misrepresentation or nondisclosure that renders existing statements misleading, and Basic reiterates that “silence, absent a duty to disclose, is not misleading under Rule 10b-5.” Treating Item 303 as automatically creating private 10b-5 liability would expand the implied private right beyond the statute’s text and risk undermining institutional legitimacy by converting a complex disclosure regime primarily enforced by the SEC into a broad damages remedy. A narrower, precedent-consistent rule is that Item 303 omissions may be relevant where they create a half-truth, but not actionable “by itself” under §10(b) and Rule 10b-5.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 10(b) by its text reaches only “manipulative or deceptive” devices, and Rule 10b-5(b) likewise targets untrue statements or omissions only when “necessary in order to make the statements made … not misleading,” not stand-alone regulatory noncompliance. Under Santa Fe Industries, Inc. v. Green, this Court has refused to judicially extend §10(b) and Rule 10b-5 beyond deception into broader corporate or regulatory wrongs, and a bare Item 303 omission—untethered to any misleading affirmative statement—falls outside that limited scope. Congress knew how to impose liability for omitting facts “required to be stated” (as in Securities Act §11), and it did not do so in §10(b); allowing private plaintiffs to convert Item 303 into a freestanding §10(b) duty would expand liability beyond the statute’s original public meaning and the Act’s enforcement structure. Basic’s statement that “silence, absent a duty to disclose, is not misleading” does not authorize importing any SEC disclosure rule into §10(b) private fraud absent deception, especially where the omission does not render any statement a half-truth.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Rule 10b‑5(b) targets misstatements and misleading half-truths; it does not, by its text, create private liability for a pure omission untethered to any affirmative statement rendered misleading. Reading Item 303’s MD&A requirement as automatically supplying a freestanding “duty to disclose” enforceable via private §10(b) actions would expand implied liability beyond §10(b)’s structure and blur Congress’s distinct choice in Securities Act §11 to expressly impose liability for omitting facts “required to be stated.” Our omission cases like Chiarella v. United States recognize a duty-to-disclose framework grounded in fiduciary or similar relationships, not a sweeping conversion of regulatory disclosure obligations into fraud absent a misleading statement. As a practical matter, allowing private 10b‑5 suits for standalone Item 303 omissions would invite hindsight pleading and over-deterrence in an area the Exchange Act largely entrusts to SEC enforcement and calibrated judgment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 are aimed at deceptive conduct—misstatements and misleading half-truths—not at enforcing every regulatory disclosure lapse through private fraud suits, and this Court has repeatedly tied omission liability to a distinct duty whose breach makes silence deceptive. Under Chiarella v. United States and Dirks v. SEC, silence becomes actionable only when there is a duty to disclose arising from a relationship of trust or a need to avoid misleading investors, not merely because an agency rule requires additional discussion in MD&A. Allowing Item 303 “required to be stated” omissions to stand alone as 10b-5 claims risks collapsing the careful statutory structure—where Congress expressly created omission liability in Securities Act §11—into an open-ended, hindsight-driven private enforcement regime that §10(b)’s text and Santa Fe Industries, Inc. v. Green caution against. Plaintiffs remain protected where the omission renders an affirmative statement misleading, but a pure Item 303 violation should be addressed primarily through SEC enforcement rather than expanding implied private liability under §10(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 10b‑5(b) targets “untrue statement[s]” and omissions only when “necessary in order to make the statements made… not misleading,” so a standalone Item 303 lapse that does not render any affirmative statement misleading falls outside the text and structure of §10(b) and Rule 10b‑5. Our cases treat omissions as actionable in private 10b‑5 suits only where there is a duty to disclose tied to the “ever-present duty not to mislead,” not as a freestanding federal cause of action for violating a disclosure rule. Basic and Matrixx cabin liability through materiality and the anti-“mountain of useless information” concern, which would be undermined by converting Item 303’s management-focused MD&A regime into automatic private-fraud exposure. The more workable and coherent approach is to leave Item 303 enforcement primarily to the SEC and to allow private 10b‑5 liability only for affirmative misstatements or half-truths, consistent with Santa Fe’s warning against expanding §10(b) beyond fraud.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5(b) target fraud in connection with the purchase or sale of securities, and—consistent with common-law fraud principles—treat “pure omissions” as actionable only when there is a duty to disclose arising from a special relationship (as in insider trading) or when needed to avoid making an affirmative statement misleading (a half-truth). Chiarella v. United States and Dirks v. SEC make clear that silence is not fraud absent such a duty, and nothing in the text of §10(b) or Rule 10b-5 creates a private cause of action for every violation of an SEC line-item disclosure rule. Allowing Item 303 (an SEC regulatory disclosure requirement) to supply, by itself, the predicate for private 10b-5 liability would expand implied private enforcement beyond the statutory text and upset separation-of-powers limits recognized in cases like Santa Fe Industries v. Green. Plaintiffs remain free to pursue 10b-5 claims where an Item 303 omission renders an affirmative statement misleading, but a standalone Item 303 omission should not suffice.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rule 10b-5(b) targets misleading statements and half-truths—an “omit[ting] to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made … not misleading”—and does not create freestanding private liability for failing to include information merely “required to be stated” by an SEC disclosure rule like Item 303. That textual and structural contrast with Securities Act §11, which expressly reaches omissions of facts “required to be stated,” reinforces that Congress calibrated different regimes and that courts should not expand the implied §10(b) action beyond deception. Our omission cases like Chiarella and Dirks ground §10(b) omission liability in a duty that makes silence deceptive in context (typically fiduciary or similar), not in every regulatory noncompliance, and Santa Fe cautions against converting §10(b) into a broad federal corporate-disclosure code. As a practical matter, allowing standalone Item 303 omissions to support private §10(b) claims would invite uncertain, hindsight-driven litigation over MD&A judgments and undermine workability and predictability in the securities-fraud framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5(b) by their terms target deceptive conduct and misleading statements, and this Court has repeatedly resisted converting federal securities law into a general disclosure code untethered to deception. Under Chiarella v. United States, silence is actionable only where there is an independent duty to disclose arising from a relationship of trust and confidence or where disclosure is necessary to avoid making what was said misleading; a regulatory reporting obligation like Item 303 does not itself supply the kind of fiduciary-like duty that makes nondisclosure “fraud” under §10(b). Treating every Item 303 violation as privately actionable would expand implied private liability beyond the statutory text and methodological limits emphasized in Santa Fe Industries, Inc. v. Green, and it would bypass the SEC’s chosen enforcement framework for MD&A disclosures. Plaintiffs remain able to proceed under a traditional “half-truth” theory when an issuer’s affirmative statements are rendered misleading by omitted trend information, but a pure Item 303 omission alone is not enough under Rule 10b-5.

SEC), an Item 303 violation—without any misleading affirmative statement—does not itself supply the kind of deception §10(b) requires. Moreover, Basic Inc. v. Levinson’s materiality framework for contingent information under Rule 10b-5 does not mirror Item 303’s MD&A regime, and treating every Item 303 omission as potentially privately actionable risks overdeterrence and undermines predictable, fair notice for issuers while the SEC remains the primary enforcer of its disclosure rules. case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an issuer’s omission of information required by SEC Regulation S‑K Item 303 (MD&A) can, by itself and without making any other statement misleading, support a private antifraud claim under Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b‑5.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and SEC Rule 10b‑5 (with the alleged duty to disclose arising from SEC Regulation S‑K, Item 303).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Rule 10b‑5 liability for omissions exists only when silence makes an affirmative statement misleading (a classic half‑truth) or when another recognized disclosure duty applies; a standalone failure to provide Item 303 MD&A disclosure is a regulatory reporting violation that does not automatically equate to securities “fraud.” They contend the Second Circuit improperly converted Item 303 into an expansive, judge‑made private right of action under §10(b), contradicting other circuits, and that this expansion undermines PSLRA limits by inviting hindsight pleading and litigation over managerial judgments about trends and uncertainties.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Moab) maintain that Item 303 imposes a mandatory disclosure duty about known trends/uncertainties reasonably likely to materially affect financial results; once that duty exists, omission of the required information can qualify as an actionable omission under Rule 10b‑5—so long as plaintiffs independently plead all other elements of a §10(b) claim (materiality, scienter, reliance, loss causation, etc.). Respondent Barclays (sued under Securities Act §§11 and 12(a)(2)) notes the Court’s answer may also affect Securities Act claims premised on the same Item 303 omissions, because those provisions more readily allow liability for material omissions in offering documents and prospectuses.
key_precedents: Leidos, Inc. v. Indiana Public Retirement System

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Item 303 is mandatory and investors expect SEC reports to be complete, so omission of a known trend feels “deceptive.” But as Justice Kagan stresses, Rule 10b-5(b) limits omission liability to what is necessary “to make the statements made … not misleading,” and the Exchange Act’s structure—especially Congress’s express “required to be stated” omission language in Securities Act §11—counsels against converting a line-item reporting duty into an implied private antifraud cause of action. Justice Alito’s PSLRA point reinforces a narrow, workable rule: plaintiffs must tie the omission to a specific misleading statement, not plead a standalone MD&A noncompliance theory. Consistent with Chiarella/Dirks (as Justice Gorsuch notes), I would hold only that Item 303 violations are not automatically actionable under §10(b), while preserving liability for half-truths where the omitted Item 303 information renders affirmative statements misleading.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that Item 303 creates a duty to disclose and that breaching a duty can be “deceptive,” but §10(b) by its text targets “manipulative or deceptive” devices and Rule 10b-5(b) reaches omissions only when needed to make “the statements made” not misleading—i.e., half-truths, not freestanding regulatory noncompliance. As Justice Roberts notes, Congress knew how to create express private liability for omitting facts “required to be stated” (e.g., §11), and we should not use an implied §10(b) action to replicate that standard by judicial expansion. The Chiarella/Dirks duty-to-speak principle cited by Justice Gorsuch confirms that silence becomes fraud only when the duty arises from the antifraud provision’s own contours (special relationship or misleading speech), not merely from an SEC line-item disclosure rule. Item 303 can inform whether an affirmative statement is misleading, but treating every Item 303 omission as actionable would exceed the original public meaning of “deceptive” in §10(b) and contravene our limits on implied private rights recognized in Central Bank and Stoneridge.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that Item 303 creates a mandatory disclosure duty and that, under Basic, material omissions can be actionable; but Basic and Matrixx address materiality once a disclosure obligation exists and do not erase Rule 10b-5(b)’s textual limit to omissions “necessary in order to make the statements made… not misleading.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, reading §10(b) to impose standalone liability for any “required to be stated” omission would effectively import Securities Act §11’s express standard into a different statute with different text, while also weakening PSLRA pleading discipline by shifting cases into omission-only theories untethered to a misleading statement. Chiarella’s baseline remains that silence is not deception absent a duty rooted in the antifraud provision’s own contours (a special relationship or a half-truth), not merely a line-item disclosure rule. Item 303 can still matter as the omitted fact that makes an affirmative statement misleading, but its violation alone should not satisfy §10(b)’s deception element in a private suit.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that Item 303’s mandatory MD&A regime exists to protect ordinary investors and that a known-trend omission in a periodic report feels like the kind of harmful silence §10(b) should deter. But Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Rule 10b-5(b)’s text—omissions are actionable only when necessary to make “the statements made” not misleading—matters for both fair notice and workable pleading boundaries, especially with Item 303’s inherently judgment-laden “trends and uncertainties.” Justice Kagan’s structural comparison to Securities Act §11 is also persuasive: Congress expressly created “required to be stated” private liability there, and I’m reluctant (even given real-world investor harms) to convert an SEC line-item disclosure rule into an implied private antifraud duty that collapses that statutory distinction. Item 303 can and should inform half-truth analysis, and robust SEC enforcement remains available, but a freestanding Item 303 omission theory risks hindsight-driven litigation without a clear deception hook under Chiarella’s duty-to-speak baseline.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Item 303 is mandatory and investors expect Exchange Act reports to be complete, so an omission could feel “misleading.” But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Rule 10b-5(b) textually limits omission liability to what is “necessary… to make the statements made… not misleading,” which maps onto half-truths rather than a freestanding “required to be stated” regime—especially given Congress’s explicit use of that latter formulation in Securities Act §11. Justice Kavanaugh’s workability concerns reinforce the textual reading: converting MD&A’s predictive “known trends and uncertainties” judgments into automatic private-fraud liability would invite hindsight pleading and effectively privatize enforcement of line-item rules in tension with Chiarella’s duty-to-speak baseline. Item 303 can still do meaningful work by identifying facts whose omission makes affirmative statements misleading under Basic/Matrixx materiality, but it cannot, standing alone, supply the deception element for a private §10(b) claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Item 303 creates a mandatory disclosure duty and that breaching that duty should be “deceptive” for §10(b) purposes, but that argument runs into the text of Rule 10b-5(b), which limits omission liability to what is “necessary in order to make the statements made … not misleading,” i.e., half-truths rather than freestanding incompleteness. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural comparison to Securities Act §11 is decisive under a textualist approach: Congress expressly imposed liability for omitting facts “required to be stated” there, and we should not import that standard into an implied §10(b) action. Chiarella/Dirks supply the common-law baseline that silence is not fraud absent a duty arising from a relationship of trust or from having spoken misleadingly; an SEC line-item rule may warrant SEC enforcement but does not itself satisfy §10(b)’s deception element for private suits. I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh that Item 303 can still matter as the omitted fact that makes an affirmative statement misleading, but noncompliance alone is not automatically actionable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—that Item 303’s mandatory MD&A regime creates a disclosure duty whose breach is itself “deceptive”—still runs into the textual limit of Rule 10b-5(b), which addresses omissions only when necessary to make “the statements made” not misleading, i.e., the half-truth framework. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point about Congress expressly creating “required to be stated” omissions liability in Securities Act §11, but not in §10(b), reinforces that we should not expand the implied private right to become a general enforcement mechanism for line-item disclosure rules. Justice Jackson’s workability concern is also persuasive: standalone Item 303 liability would invite hindsight litigation over management’s judgment about “trends and uncertainties” and dilute PSLRA discipline, while preserving SEC enforcement and traditional half-truth claims. No colleague has identified precedent that squarely holds that regulatory noncompliance alone—absent a misleading statement—satisfies the deception element under §10(b), so my vote remains for petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that Item 303 creates a mandatory duty and investors rely on the completeness of SEC filings—does not satisfy Rule 10b-5(b)’s textual trigger, which attaches omission liability only when necessary to make “the statements made” not misleading. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural comparison to Securities Act §11 is decisive under a textualist approach: Congress expressly created liability for omitting facts “required to be stated” there, but did not use that formulation in §10(b), so we should not replicate §11 by implication through a judge-made cause of action. Chiarella/Dirks, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, reinforce the baseline that silence becomes “deceptive” only when tied to a relationship-based duty or to a half-truth created by what the speaker chose to say; a line-item regulation may inform what counts as misleading, but it cannot alone supply deception. I therefore remain persuaded that Item 303 can be evidentiary in assessing whether affirmative statements were misleading, but noncompliance with Item 303 is not independently actionable under §10(b)/Rule 10b-5(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that Item 303’s mandatory MD&A duty makes an omission “deceptive” because investors expect completeness in periodic reports—still runs into Rule 10b-5(b)’s limiting text, which (as Chief Justice Roberts stresses) treats omissions as actionable only when needed to make “statements made” not misleading, not as a freestanding enforcement hook for line-item rules. Justice Kagan’s structural comparison to Securities Act §11 is especially persuasive for me as a pragmatic matter of fair notice and institutional competence: Congress used an explicit “required to be stated” omission standard when it wanted that kind of liability, and importing it into §10(b) would expand implied private enforcement in a way that predictably invites hindsight pleading over MD&A judgments. Chiarella/Dirks, highlighted by Justice Gorsuch, also reinforces that the “duty to speak” in private antifraud suits must be anchored in the antifraud framework (or a half-truth), not merely in regulatory incompleteness. I remain convinced Item 303 can and should inform half-truth analysis—preserving investor protection—without converting every MD&A shortfall into §10(b) deception and weakening the PSLRA’s pleading discipline.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 10b‑5(b) targets misleading statements and omissions that render what was said misleading; absent a half-truth or some other recognized duty to disclose under the antifraud rule itself, a standalone failure to provide Item 303 MD&A disclosure is regulatory noncompliance, not automatically actionable private fraud under §10(b). This narrower reading accords with Chiarella v. United States and its progeny requiring a duty to disclose before omission liability attaches, and it avoids using §10(b) to create a de facto private right to enforce SEC line-item reporting rules. A holding for petitioners can be narrow: Item 303 omissions may still support §10(b) liability when they make other statements misleading, but not “by themselves” without a misleading statement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of §10(b) targets “manipulative or deceptive” devices, and Rule 10b‑5(b) separately forbids omitting a material fact only when necessary “to make the statements made … not misleading,” which does not encompass a freestanding regulatory reporting lapse under Item 303. Treating every Item 303 omission as actionable would improperly expand the implied private right under §10(b) beyond what the statute’s text prohibits, a step this Court has rejected in Central Bank of Denver and reiterated in Stoneridge. Item 303 may create an administrative disclosure obligation enforceable by the SEC, but absent a misleading half-truth, it does not by itself supply the deception element required for a private 10b‑5 antifraud claim. Accordingly, the Second Circuit’s approach should be rejected as inconsistent with the statute’s original public meaning and this Court’s limits on implied liability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 10b‑5(b) targets omissions only when they render an affirmative statement misleading (“in order to make the statements made… not misleading”), not stand-alone failures to provide information “required to be stated” by an SEC reporting rule like Item 303. Reading §10(b) to impose private liability for any Item 303 omission would effectively create a broad, judge-made cause of action to enforce disclosure regulations, contrary to the Exchange Act’s structure and the careful, express omissions liability Congress created elsewhere (e.g., Securities Act §11). The PSLRA reinforces this narrower view by requiring plaintiffs to identify specific misleading statements and why they are misleading, which a pure Item 303-omission theory bypasses. Basic does not compel a contrary result; it addresses materiality and reliance in the presence of a duty to disclose, but it does not transform regulatory noncompliance into §10(b) fraud absent a misleading half-truth.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Chiarella and Basic, Rule 10b‑5 omission liability generally requires a duty to disclose that arises because an issuer’s silence makes an affirmative statement misleading (a half-truth), not merely because an SEC reporting rule was violated. Item 303 creates an important regulatory disclosure obligation enforceable by the SEC, but §10(b) and Rule 10b‑5 do not, like Securities Act §11, expressly authorize private suits for omitting facts “required to be stated,” and we should not expand private antifraud liability beyond the rule’s text and structure. Matrixx confirms that materiality is not a bright-line inquiry, yet it does not convert every regulatory disclosure duty into a freestanding antifraud duty absent misleading speech. Preserving a clear line protects fair notice and prevents hindsight-driven litigation that would distort managerial disclosure judgments, while leaving robust public enforcement and classic half-truth claims to protect investors, including vulnerable retirees.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Text and structure point against treating Item 303 as automatically creating a privately enforceable omission duty under §10(b) and Rule 10b-5(b): Rule 10b-5(b) is framed around making an untrue statement or omitting facts “necessary in order to make the statements made … not misleading,” which fits classic half-truth liability rather than freestanding regulatory noncompliance. Reading §10(b) to cover pure Item 303 omissions would also blur the deliberate statutory contrast with Securities Act §11, which expressly imposes liability for omitting facts “required to be stated,” and would effectively convert SEC disclosure rules into a broad private cause of action inconsistent with the Exchange Act’s enforcement scheme. Chiarella’s duty-to-disclose principle reinforces that silence becomes fraud only when there is a recognized duty rooted in the antifraud provision itself (often via half-truths or special relationships), not simply because another regulation requires disclosure. That leaves room for §10(b) claims where Item 303 information is omitted in a way that renders other affirmative statements misleading (as in Basic/Matrixx materiality analysis), while keeping Item 303’s standalone enforcement primarily with the SEC.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 10(b) targets the use of a “manipulative or deceptive device,” and Rule 10b‑5(b) likewise forbids omissions only when they render “the statements made” misleading; a bare Item 303 reporting lapse, untethered to any misleading half-truth, is not deception within the statute’s plain terms. Our omission cases, including Chiarella v. United States and Dirks v. SEC, reflect the common-law baseline that silence is actionable only when there is a recognized duty to speak (typically arising from a special relationship of trust/confidence or from having spoken in a way that would mislead), not merely because an agency requires disclosure in periodic filings. Treating Item 303 as independently actionable under §10(b) would effectively create an additional, judge-made private right of action for regulatory noncompliance, raising serious separation-of-powers concerns and expanding liability beyond what Congress prescribed in the Exchange Act and the PSLRA framework. Plaintiffs remain protected against fraud through classic half-truth liability under Rule 10b‑5(b), but Item 303 alone cannot supply “deception” for §10(b) purposes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rule 10b-5(b) targets false statements and misleading half-truths, not stand-alone “pure omissions” absent an independent duty to disclose that makes existing statements misleading; this Court has repeatedly emphasized that “silence” is actionable only where there is such a duty and the omission renders what was said misleading. See Basic Inc. v. Levinson, 485 U.S. 224, 239–40 & n.18 (1988), and Matrixx Initiatives, Inc. v. Siracusano, 563 U.S. 27, 44 (2011). Treating a Regulation S-K Item 303 reporting obligation as automatically creating private §10(b) liability would effectively expand Rule 10b-5 beyond its text and our precedents, invite hindsight litigation over managerial judgments about “trends and uncertainties,” and undermine the PSLRA’s gatekeeping and the practical workability of securities-fraud pleading standards. Item 303 remains enforceable by the SEC, and plaintiffs can still proceed under §10(b) when an Item 303 omission also results in a misleading half-truth, but the regulatory omission alone should not suffice.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Rule 10b-5(b) targets omissions only when necessary “to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading,” which reflects the settled distinction between actionable half-truths and nonactionable pure nondisclosure absent an independent duty. Under Chiarella v. United States and its progeny, §10(b) does not create a freestanding duty to disclose; duties arise from specific relationships or from speaking in a way that would be misleading without additional facts. Treating an Item 303 reporting violation as automatically actionable under §10(b) would effectively import Section 11’s “required to be stated” omission standard into the Exchange Act, contrary to the differing statutory texts and the Exchange Act’s structure and enforcement scheme. Plaintiffs may still proceed where the Item 303 matter renders affirmative statements misleading, but the omission alone cannot supply §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 liability.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 are antifraud provisions, and this Court has repeatedly emphasized that “silence, absent a duty to disclose, is not misleading” and that omission liability typically attaches when needed to avoid making an affirmative statement a misleading half-truth. Reading SEC Regulation S-K Item 303’s MD&A requirements to create a freestanding private 10b-5 omission theory would effectively convert a disclosure-regulation violation into securities “fraud,” expanding private liability beyond the text and structure Congress reinforced through the PSLRA’s requirement that a complaint identify each misleading statement and why it was misleading. Practical consequences also counsel restraint: allowing Item 303-alone claims would invite hindsight pleading about managerial judgments on “trends and uncertainties,” increase omission-only class actions, and leverage the Affiliated Ute reliance presumption in ways that dilute procedural fairness protections at the pleading stage. Item 303 can still matter when its omission renders other statements misleading (a classic half-truth), but not as a standalone basis for Rule 10b-5 liability.
